claims.text: Equimolar Mo, W, V, Nb, and Ta dithiocarbamate precursors provide a molecular-scale disordered mixture for producing (MoWVNbTa)S2.
Thermolysis at 500 °C for 1 hour under 300 cm3 min−1 argon will form a high-entropy disulfide powder.
SPS at 1000 °C for 15 minutes under 30 MPa can consolidate the thermolyzed powder.
The resulting (MoWVNbTa)S2 material will have a stable, single-phase 2H crystal structure.
The single-phase material will possess high configurational entropy and significant lattice distortion.
High configurational entropy and lattice distortion prevent Nb and Ta segregation and stabilize the matrix against high-temperature phase decomposition.
Atomic-scale mixing from the molecular-precursor route prevents secondary-phase formation during low-temperature decomposition.
SPS at 1000 °C promotes densification and grain growth in (MoWVNbTa)S2.
Entropy of mixing and metal-size mismatch kinetically inhibit diffusion-driven phase separation during SPS.
Suppression of phase separation locks in a hard, dense, and corrosion-resistant structure.
The bulk (MoWVNbTa)S2 material will exhibit Vickers hardness exceeding 450 HV.
SPS will produce a bulk density approaching the theoretical density of (MoWVNbTa)S2.
The material will have a lower aqueous corrosion current density than standard FeCoCrNi high-entropy alloys.
A stable protective oxide layer on the 2H lattice surface causes the predicted corrosion resistance.
An FeCoCrNi composite containing 30 wt.% WC has a microhardness of 459.2 HV.
The FeCoCrNi–30 wt.% WC baseline potentially has lower oxidation resistance because of carbide interfaces and the absence of a sulfide-derived protective-oxide mechanism.
The SPS temperature must remain below 1100 °C to prevent decomposition of the disulfide into oxides or elemental metals.
Strictly equimolar precursor mixing is required to maintain the high-entropy state.
Failure to achieve atomic-scale precursor mixing will cause elemental segregation and loss of single-phase stability.

contradictions.description: The predicted corrosion resistance is attributed to formation of a protective oxide layer, while the falsification rule treats detection of secondary oxides after high-temperature exposure as sufficient to falsify the hypothesis. The rule does not distinguish a beneficial surface oxide from detrimental bulk oxide phases.
